headline: ADNOC Gas heads for 15.6 million tonnes with India as its anchor market
deck: A ten-year, $3bn agreement with HPCL converted a heads of agreement into a binding contract and put 0.5 million tonnes a year into Gujarat.
excerpt: ADNOC Gas expects to operate 15.6 million tonnes a year of LNG capacity by 2029, with 3.2 million tonnes contracted to Indian buyers. Its ten-year agreement with Hindustan Petroleum is the template for how the Emirates is placing volumes ahead of Ruwais.
content:
Gastech opens in Bangkok this week with Asian demand as its organising theme, and the Emirates arrives with the clearest picture of where its volumes are going.

ADNOC Gas signed a ten-year liquefied natural gas sales and purchase agreement with Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited valued at approximately $2.5bn to $3bn, covering 0.5 million tonnes a year. The agreement converted a previously announced heads of agreement into a binding contract, and was announced during a state visit to India by the UAE President.

The volumes are supplied from ADNOC Gas's Das Island liquefaction facility, which has production capacity of up to 6 million tonnes a year and is one of the world's longest-operating LNG plants. HPCL receives the cargoes at its 5 million tonne a year import and regasification terminal at Chhara in Gujarat.

The company expects to be operating 15.6 million tonnes a year of LNG capacity by 2029, with 3.2 million tonnes contracted to Indian buyers including HPCL. India is described as the Emirates' largest LNG customer.

Several things in that structure repay attention from an industrial standpoint.

The first is that this is a trade built on existing assets rather than announced ones. Das Island has been liquefying gas for decades, and volumes contracted from an operating plant carry none of the construction risk attached to capacity still being built.

The second is the receiving terminal. An LNG sale is only as firm as the buyer's ability to take delivery, and a regasification terminal is a substantial piece of infrastructure in its own right: berth, unloading arms, cryogenic storage, vaporisers and a connection into a gas grid. The Chhara terminal's 5 million tonne capacity is what makes a 0.5 million tonne annual commitment executable.

The third is the shape of the market this describes. Ten-year terms at half a million tonnes a year are mid-sized contracts, well below the twenty-year, multi-million tonne agreements that characterised earlier LNG cycles. Buyers in growth markets have been pressing for shorter durations and more flexibility, and sellers with capacity to place have been accommodating it.

That matters for Ruwais LNG, which adds 9.6 million tonnes a year from 2028 and has long-term commitments already above 90 per cent of capacity, with close to 23 per cent going to Japanese customers. Placing that volume in a market that no longer signs twenty-year deals as a matter of course is the commercial achievement, and it was done before commissioning rather than after.

Gastech runs at BITEC Bangkok from 14 to 17 September.

For the Gulf's engineering base the interest is at the receiving end as much as the exporting one. Regasification terminals, storage tanks, cryogenic pipework and jetty infrastructure are being built across South and Southeast Asia to take these volumes, and they draw on the same specialist contractors and cryogenic equipment makers that the liquefaction side does.
author: Jakson Gudawela
scheduledReason: Written before Gastech opens on 14 September. It analyses publicly announced contracts and capacity figures, and reports nothing from the event.
